modules.title: 1 · Targets, transformations, and stationarity
modules.summary: Define the forecasting target before choosing a model.

stages.title: Targets, transformations, and stationarity: research guide
stages.html:
Targets, transformations, and stationarity

Define the forecasting target before choosing a model.

Logs, differences, seasonal adjustments, and levels change the estimand; every forecast must be transformed back consistently.

Workflow. Choose levels, logs, differences, or seasonal adjustments for the forecasting target.

Diagnostic: Inspect units, trend, seasonality, and invertibility. The main failure to avoid is a forecast evaluated on a scale different from the decision target.

stages.title: Series transformations intuition lab
stages.note: Drag the Box-Cox power λ. Watch the variance of the first vs second half of the series equalise as λ→0 (the log) — the transform picks the scale on which the target is well-behaved.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 240
t = np.arange(n)
level = np.exp(0.012 * t)                       # smooth exponential trend
y = level * np.exp(0.35 * rng.normal(0, 1, n))  # multiplicative error grows with level
lam = {{lam}}
z = (np.power(y, lam) - 1) / lam if abs(lam) > 1e-6 else np.log(y)
half = n // 2
v1, v2 = z[:half].var(), z[half:].var()          # variance homogeneity check
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(t, z, color="#da9100", lw=1.2)
plt.axvline(half, color="#c9c6ac", ls="--", lw=1)
plt.xlabel("time"); plt.ylabel(f"Box-Cox(y, lambda={lam:g})")
plt.title(f"var(early)={v1:.3f}   var(late)={v2:.3f}   ratio={v2/v1:.2f}")
print(f"lambda={lam:g}: variance ratio (late/early) = {v2/v1:.2f}  (near 1 = stabilised)")
print("lambda=0 (log) turns multiplicative errors additive; forecasts must be back-transformed on this scale")

stages.note: Run the reproducible example, then change one assumption and compare the output.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
phi = 0.72
y = np.zeros(160)
for t in range(1, len(y)):
    y[t] = phi*y[t-1] + rng.normal(scale=0.8)
X, target = y[:-1, None], y[1:]
phi_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(X, target, rcond=None)[0][0]
forecast = phi_hat*y[-1]
print(f"Estimated persistence: {phi_hat:.3f}")
print(f"One-step forecast: {forecast:.3f}")

modules.title: 2 · ACF, PACF, and dependence
modules.summary: Read sample correlation patterns as evidence, not an automatic order selector.

stages.title: ACF, PACF, and dependence: research guide
stages.html:
ACF, PACF, and dependence

Read sample correlation patterns as evidence, not an automatic order selector.

Autocorrelation diagnostics are noisy and should be combined with a plausible data process, residual checks, and forecast validation.

Workflow. Distinguish deterministic trend, unit-root persistence, and stationary dynamics.

Diagnostic: Inspect rolling moments, roots, and unit-root evidence. The main failure to avoid is spurious autocorrelation and unreliable long-horizon forecasts.

stages.title: Univariate stationarity intuition lab
stages.note: Drag the AR persistence φ. The orange sample ACF wobbles around the smooth population curve φ^k, and several spikes past lag 5 pierce the dashed bands purely from sampling noise — evidence, not a mechanical order rule.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 160
phi = {{phi}}
y = np.zeros(n)
for k in range(1, n):
    y[k] = phi * y[k-1] + rng.normal(0, 1)
nlags = 20
r = acf(y, nlags=nlags, fft=False)
band = 1.96 / np.sqrt(n)                          # white-noise sampling band
theo = phi ** np.arange(nlags + 1)               # population ACF of AR(1)
spurious = int(np.sum(np.abs(r[6:]) > band))     # lags 6+ are ~0 in truth
lags = np.arange(nlags + 1)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.vlines(lags, 0, r, color="#da9100", lw=3)
plt.plot(lags, theo, "o-", color="#5b8a72", ms=3, lw=1, label="population phi^k")
plt.axhline(band, color="#c9c6ac", ls="--", lw=1)
plt.axhline(-band, color="#c9c6ac", ls="--", lw=1)
plt.axhline(0, color="#888", lw=0.8)
plt.xlabel("lag"); plt.ylabel("sample ACF"); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f"phi={phi:g}: {spurious} spikes cross the band past lag 5 (all noise)")
print(f"lag-1 sample ACF = {r[1]:.3f}   population phi = {phi:g}")
print(f"{spurious} spurious spikes exceed +/-{band:.3f} past lag 5 -- diagnostics are noisy")

modules.title: 3 · ARMA dynamics
modules.summary: Combine persistent states with transitory innovations.

stages.title: ARMA dynamics: research guide
stages.html:
ARMA dynamics

Combine persistent states with transitory innovations.

Autoregressive terms propagate past outcomes; moving-average terms propagate past innovations, subject to stability and invertibility.

Workflow. Use correlation patterns as model clues rather than mechanical identification rules.

Diagnostic: Inspect sampling bands, residual ACF, and plausible alternatives. The main failure to avoid is overconfident order selection from noisy sample spikes.

stages.title: ACF and PACF diagnostics intuition lab
stages.note: Set the AR φ and MA θ. The bars are the impulse response (MA(∞) weights): θ lifts the lag-1 response, then φ decays every horizon geometrically — persistent state vs transitory innovation.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.arima_process import ArmaProcess
phi = {{phi}}
theta = {{theta}}
proc = ArmaProcess(np.array([1, -phi]), np.array([1, theta]))
h = 16
irf = proc.arma2ma(lags=h)                        # MA(inf) weights = response to a unit shock
lags = np.arange(h)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.vlines(lags, 0, irf, color="#da9100", lw=3)
plt.plot(lags, phi ** lags, "o-", color="#5b8a72", ms=3, lw=1, label="pure AR (phi^k)")
plt.axhline(0, color="#888", lw=0.8)
plt.xlabel("horizon k"); plt.ylabel("response to a unit shock")
plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f"ARMA(1,1) phi={phi:g}, theta={theta:g}   stable={proc.isstationary}")
print(f"impulse response: psi0={irf[0]:.2f}, psi1={irf[1]:.2f}, psi2={irf[2]:.2f}")
print(f"MA adds {theta:g} at lag 1; AR then decays every horizon at rate {phi:g}")

modules.title: 4 · ARIMA and seasonal structure
modules.summary: Difference parsimoniously and model the remaining dynamics.

stages.title: ARIMA and seasonal structure: research guide
stages.html:
ARIMA and seasonal structure

Difference parsimoniously and model the remaining dynamics.

Overdifferencing amplifies noise; underdifferencing leaves persistent residual structure and unstable long-horizon uncertainty.

Workflow. Represent persistent shocks with autoregressive and moving-average terms.

Diagnostic: Inspect root conditions, innovation definition, and parsimony. The main failure to avoid is noninvertible or unstable dynamics.

stages.title: ARMA dynamics intuition lab
stages.note: Drag the differencing order d applied to a random walk. d=1 whitens it; d=2 or more overdifferences — variance climbs and the lag-1 autocorrelation is pushed toward -0.5, the classic overdifferencing symptom.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 300
eps = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = np.cumsum(eps)            # I(1) random walk: exactly one difference is correct
d = int({{d}})
w = y.copy()
for _ in range(d):
    w = np.diff(w)
lag1 = acf(w, nlags=1, fft=False)[1] if len(w) > 2 else float("nan")
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.plot(w, color="#da9100", lw=1)
plt.axhline(0, color="#888", lw=0.8)
plt.xlabel("time"); plt.ylabel(f"(1-L)^{d} y")
plt.title(f"d={d}: var={w.var():.2f}   lag-1 ACF={lag1:.2f}")
print(f"d={d}: variance={w.var():.3f}, lag-1 autocorr={lag1:.3f}")
print("d=1 whitens the walk; d>=2 overdifferences -> variance rises, lag-1 ACF -> -0.5")

modules.title: 5 · Rolling-origin forecast evaluation
modules.summary: Judge forecasts using information that was genuinely available at each origin.

stages.title: Rolling-origin forecast evaluation: research guide
stages.html:
Rolling-origin forecast evaluation

Judge forecasts using information that was genuinely available at each origin.

A benchmark, horizon, estimation window, and loss function must be fixed before comparing models out of sample.

Workflow. Demand approximately innovation-like residuals and stable parameters.

Diagnostic: Inspect residual ACF, variance shifts, and structural breaks. The main failure to avoid is a fitted model that leaves predictable information unused.

stages.title: Forecast diagnostics intuition lab
stages.note: Set the true persistence φ and the rolling estimation window. Each origin re-fits AR(1) on only its own past and forecasts one step; the bars compare its out-of-sample RMSE against the random-walk benchmark that was fixed in advance.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 220
phi = {{phi}}
y = np.zeros(n)
for k in range(1, n):
    y[k] = phi * y[k-1] + rng.normal(0, 1)
win = int({{win}})
err_ar, err_naive = [], []
for o in range(win, n - 1):               # each origin uses only information up to o
    past = y[o-win:o]
    b = np.dot(past[:-1], past[1:]) / np.dot(past[:-1], past[:-1])  # AR(1) fit on the window
    err_ar.append(y[o+1] - b * y[o])      # 1-step AR forecast
    err_naive.append(y[o+1] - y[o])       # random-walk benchmark
rmse_ar = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(err_ar)))
rmse_naive = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(err_naive)))
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.bar(["AR(1) rolling", "naive (RW)"], [rmse_ar, rmse_naive], color=["#da9100", "#c9c6ac"])
plt.ylabel("out-of-sample RMSE")
plt.title(f"phi={phi:g}, window={win}: benchmark/model = {rmse_naive/rmse_ar:.2f}x")
print(f"rolling-origin RMSE  AR(1)={rmse_ar:.3f}  naive={rmse_naive:.3f}")
print("only each origin's past is used; benchmark, horizon and window are fixed before comparing")
